tone_statements.citation: Nguyễn Văn Tài. 1982. Ngữ âm tiếng Mường qua các phương ngôn. Tóm tắt luận án phó tiến sĩ khoa học (author's printed summary of the candidate-of-sciences dissertation, defended 29 Oct 1983). Hà Nội: Viện Ngôn ngữ học, Ủy ban Khoa học Xã hội Việt Nam. 25 pp. (National Library of Vietnam shelfmark LA82.0135.3 / L1121t).
tone_statements.quote: 2.3.4. ... Căn cứ vào hai tiêu chí đó, có thể phân xuất hệ thống thanh điệu M.Bi thành năm thanh ... Cả 5 thanh được phân bố cho âm tiết không đóng, còn âm tiết đóng chỉ nhận thanh 3 và thanh 5. ... 3.4. Số lượng thanh điệu của tất cả các thổ ngữ có sự thống nhất tuyệt đối. Chúng tôi gặp đầy đủ năm thanh ở bất kì thổ ngữ nào, không một thổ ngữ có dấu vết bốn thanh hoặc 6 thanh. Điều đó chứng tỏ thanh điệu tiếng Mường dường như đã hoàn thành quá trình biến đổi và đang ổn định.
tone_statements.translation: 2.3.4. ... On the basis of those two criteria [register and contour] the Mường Bi tone system can be analysed into five tones ... All 5 tones are distributed over non-closed syllables, whereas closed [stop-final] syllables take only tone 3 and tone 5. ... 3.4. The number of tones is absolutely uniform across all the local varieties. We find the full five tones in every variety; not one variety shows a trace of four tones or of 6 tones. This shows that the Muong tone system seems to have completed its process of change and is stable.
tone_statements.locator: p. 9 (sec. 2.3.4, with feature table), p. 10 (top), pp. 16-17 (sec. 3.4)
tone_statements.summary: Five tones (numbered 1-5) in Mường Bi and in every Muong variety surveyed; distinctive features per the p. 9 table: register high/low(-) = 1+,2-,3-,4+,5+; glottalized/broken ('gãy') = 2,4,5 vs 1,3 (-); rising = 2,3,4 vs falling = 1,5 (as read from the typewritten table). tone_statements.citation: Barker, Milton E. 1966. Vietnamese-Muong tone correspondences. In Norman H. Zide (ed.), Studies in Comparative Austroasiatic Linguistics (Indo-Iranian Monographs 5), 9-25. The Hague: Mouton.
tone_statements.quote: With the exception of certain compounds, reduplicative patterns, and loan words, Vietnamese and Muong are both monosyllabic languages with one phonemic tone occurring on each syllable (word). ... Muong has a system of five phonemic tones: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, and high-mid level. In words with a final stop (p, t, ch, c), this five-way contrast is neutralized to a two-way contrast, the two being phonetically high rising and high-mid level. ... [fn. 7] Words with high-mid level tone without a final stop (p, t, ch, c) have a final glottal stop as an integral part of the tone, whether there is another final consonant or not.
tone_statements.locator: p. 10 and footnote 7; correspondence table p. 11
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Five phonemic tones on the syllable: mid level, low rising constricted, high rising, low falling, high-mid level (the last with final glottal stop in non-stop-final words); two-way contrast (high rising vs high-mid level) in stop-final syllables; correspondences VN ngang=M mid level, sắc(open)=low rising constricted, sắc(checked)=high rising checked, hỏi=high rising, huyền=low falling, ngã=high-m…

sources.citation: Barker, Miriam A. 1993. Bibliography of Mường and other Vietic language groups, with notes. Mon-Khmer Studies 23: 197-243.
sources.note: Page-image scan, scanned. Annotated bibliography; no entry mentions stress. Confirms Barker 1968 'The phonemes of Mương' (SiL 20: 59-62; Mường Khến dialect; 'phonemes of monosyllables: consonants, vowels, tones and sequence limitations'), Sokolovskaya & Nguyen Van Tai 1987 ('in Russian; includes a grammatical description'), Nguyen Van Tai 1983 graduate thesis (~60 varieties).

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu. 2021. Glottalization, tonal contrasts and intonation: an experimental study of the Kim Thuong dialect of Muong. PhD thesis, Université Sorbonne Nouvelle - Paris 3. 351 pp.
sources.access_detail: a digital copy (available on request); access check: open copy online
sources.note: Nothing about Muong word stress anywhere (all 'stress'/'accent' hits are generic prosody theory). Places Muong among languages with lexical tones (p. 11); 'Muong is a monosyllabic language, in the sense that a syllable = a morpheme = a word' (p. 69); function words carry lexical tone like content words (p. 76); tone inventory of Kim Thuong Muong in sect. 2.7.3 (pp. 54-60).

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu. 2016. The tone system of Kim Thượng Mường: an experimental study of fundamental frequency, duration, and phonation types. MA thesis, University of Social Sciences and Humanities, Hanoi. 164 pp.
sources.note: No stress statement. p. 21: 'Like Vietnamese, Mường is a strictly monosyllabic language from a phonological point of view: the syllable is the domain of tone'; disyllables exist in the lexicon through collocation/disyllabification.

sources.citation: Nguyễn, Minh-Châu, Lise Crevier-Buchman, Alexis Michaud & Didier Demolin. 2019. A glottalized tone in Muong (Vietic): a pilot study based on audio and electroglottographic recordings. Proc. ICPhS 2019, Melbourne. 6 pp.

sources.citation: Ferlus, Michel. 1998. Les systèmes de tons dans les langues viet-muong. Diachronica 15(1): 1-27 (HAL author version).

sources.citation: Thompson, Laurence C. (1976). Proto-Viet-Muong Phonology. In Austroasiatic Studies. Honolulu: The University Press of Hawaii. pp. 1113-1204.
sources.note: Muong is not in the catalog and has no existing stress statements; this work adds only a tone inventory for Muong Khen and is silent on word stress, consistent with the earlier-read sources in this folder (Nguyen 2016/2021: strictly monosyllabic tone language, no stress statement).

sources.note: Mường Bi has five tones defined by register (high/low), 'gãy' (glottalized/broken) and direction (rising/falling); all five occur on non-checked syllables, checked syllables take only tones 3 and 5; every Muong local variety surveyed has exactly five tones (none with four or six); dialect groups differ in the phonetic shape of tone 2 (broken vs not) and tone-1/tone-2 correspond inversely to Vietnamese ngang/huyền in one group.
